1.q: וַ⁠יֵּ֖דַע יוֹאָ֣ב בֶּן־צְרֻיָ֑ה כִּֽי־לֵ֥ב הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ עַל־אַבְשָׁלֽוֹם
1.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Here, the **heart** represents a person’s feelings. This could mean: (1) that David felt hostile toward Absalom. That is the meaning in Daniel 11:28, the only other instance of this expression in the Bible. The rest of this chapter shows that David had to be persuaded through an elaborate ruse to allow Absalom to return to Jerusalem, and even then he would not allow him to come into his presence. Alternate translation: [that King David felt hostile toward Absalom]; (2) that David was longing to see Absalom. Many versions follow this interpretation, and you may wish to follow it if a translation of the Bible exists in your region and follows it. Alternate translation: [that King David longed to see Absalom]

2.note: Putting on **clothes of mourning** and not anointing oneself **with oil** were symbolic actions that in ancient Israel showed grief and sorrow over someone who had died. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and act as if you are grieving by wearing dark clothes and not applying any oil to yourself]

Joab is not referring to a specific **woman**. He means any woman who had been **mourning many days**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like a woman]

3.note: In a context such as this, your language might say “go” instead of **come**. Alternate translation: [And you shall go]

Joab is using the term **word** to represent what he is going to say by using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and tell him the following]

Here, the author is speaking as if **words** were actually objects that Joab could have placed in the woman’s **mouth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then Joab specified what she ought to say]

4.note: The author is using a summary statement to introduce a new part of this story, which takes place in verses 4–20. Your language may have its own way of offering an introductory summary at the beginning of a new part of a story. Alternate translation: [So the Tekoite woman went to speak to the king]

Be sure that it is clear in your translation that the woman did not fall down accidentally. She knelt down in front of David, pressing her face **to the ground** as a gesture to honor him. She then **prostrated herself** or stretched out flat on the ground to show David great honor. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and she knelt on the ground in front of David, stretching herself out flat, to honor him greatly]

The woman is referring to King David by a respectful title, and she is using the customary expression of this culture to ask him to use his royal power to help her. Use a comparable title and expression from your language. Alternate translation: [Help me, Your Majesty]

5.note: The king is using **What {is} to you** as a common expression of his culture to ask the woman why she needs help. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [What is the matter]

To try to convince David that he should allow Absalom to return, the woman, as instructed by Joab, tells David a story as if it were true. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could state that explicitly. Alternate translation: [And to try to convince David to allow Absalom, she told him a story as if it were true. She said to him]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. The woman is clarifying that she is not without the support of a male relative for some other reason, for example, she has not separated from a husband who is still living. Alternate translation: [Since my husband has died, I am truly a widow]

The woman is using **a woman, a widow** as a common expression of her culture to mean “a woman who is a widow.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a woman who is a widow] or [a widow]

6.note: The woman is speaking of herself in the third person as **your maidservant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. You could translate similar expressions in the same way throughout the chapter. Alternate translation: [And to me, your maidservant]

It might seem that the expression **And the one struck him, the one** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And one of them struck the other]

7.note: The woman is using the term **behold** to call attention to what she is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. See how you translated the term “behold” in 1:2.

The woman is using **has arisen** as a common expression of her culture to mean “has taken action.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has taken action]

7.q: וַ⁠יֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ תְּנִ֣י ׀ אֶת־מַכֵּ֣ה אָחִ֗י⁠ו וּ⁠נְמִתֵ֨⁠הוּ֙ בְּ⁠נֶ֤פֶשׁ אָחִי⁠ו֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָרָ֔ג וְ⁠נַשְׁמִ֖ידָה גַּ֣ם אֶת־הַ⁠יּוֹרֵ֑שׁ
7.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and they have told me to give them the one having struck his brother so that they can kill him for the life of his brother whom he slew, and they want to destroy the heir also]
Here, **life** represents “death.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to avenge the death of his brother]

The other members of the clan would not have spoken these words directly to the woman. Since they say **let us**, in her depiction of them, they are pausing to speak confidentially to one another. They are speaking in this way because they are betraying their real motive, which is to get the late husband’s property by killing his sole remaining **heir**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate this explicitly in your translation, ending the second-level direct quotation after **he slew** and beginning a new sentence. Alternate translation: [But their real motive is to destroy the heir also]

Here, the woman is speaking as if her son were actually a **coal** that could be extinguished. She uses this image to describe her son as her family’s last remaining source of life, hope, and continuation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they would destroy my only remaining son]

The terms **name** and **remnant** mean similar things. The woman is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [any survivors]

Here, **a name** represents “someone to carry on the family line.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [anyone to carry on his name]

The woman is using one part of the earth, **the face of the ground**, to represent the entire earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [alive on earth]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:11. Alternate translation: [on the surface of the ground]

8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the king’s command with the information about the woman going home. Alternate translation: [Since I myself will command concerning you, you may go to your house]

The implication is that the king will take some action that will ensure that the woman and her son are protected. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I myself will take care of this matter for you]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will command** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is making a promise to the woman. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for this same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that David is making a promise. It may not be necessary to represent the separately stated pronoun explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I promise that I will command]

9.q: עָלַ֞⁠י אֲדֹנִ֥⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֛לֶךְ הֶ⁠עָוֺ֖ן וְ⁠עַל־בֵּ֣ית אָבִ֑⁠י
9.note: The woman is actually describing a possible condition. She is saying that if there is any wrong in this situation, she and her family, not David, will be guilty and bear the responsibility. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If there is any iniquity, my lord the king, then let it be on me and on the house of my father]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:29. Alternate translation: [my extended family]

Even though the woman is addressing the king directly, she is speaking of him in the third person as **the king and his throne** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person, here and in similar instances throughout the chapter. Alternate translation: [and may you, O king, and your throne]
Here, **throne** represents “kingdom.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and his kingdom]

10.note: The king is actually describing a possible condition. He is telling the woman that if anyone speaks to her about this matter, then she should bring that person to him. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If anyone speaks to you about this again, then bring him to me]

It might seem that the expression **he will not continue to touch you further** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and he will not continue to touch you] or [and he will not touch you further]

The king is using **he will not continue to touch you further** as a common expression of his culture to mean “he will not do any further harm to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will not do any further harm to you]

11.note: The woman is using **remember Yahweh your God** as a common expression of her culture to mean “swear an oath by Yahweh your God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you, the king, please swear an oath by Yahweh your God]

The implication is that the woman wants the king to protect her son from the avenger of blood who is trying to kill him, since that would increase the number of people who had died. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [so that the avenger of blood will not cause any further destruction of life]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Then no one will destroy my son] or [Then my son will not be destroyed]

Following the custom of his culture, David is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred. He is then stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh that not a single hair from your son will fall to the ground. If he suffers any harm, then may Yahweh punish me severely]

David is using one small part of the woman’s son, implicitly a single strand from his **hair**, to emphasize that he will not allow any harm to come to him at all. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the same expression in 1 Samuel 14:45. Alternate translation: [I swear that no one shall harm your son in the slightest way]

12.note: The woman is using the term **word** to represent what she wants to say by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [say something further]
This is an imperative, but it communicates permission rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates permission. Alternate translation: [You may speak]

13.note: The woman is using the question form to rebuke the king mildly and indirectly. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Then you should not have devised like this against the people of God.]

Here, **the people of God** represents the Israelite people, who worshiped the one true **God**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Israelite people]

Here, **word** represents the judgment that David pronounced by using words. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [For as a result of giving this judgment]

The woman is not referring to a specific **guilty** person. She means guilty people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is like a guilty person]

The expression **his banished one** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the one he has banished]

14.note: The woman is repeating forms of the verb **die** in order to intensify her expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [For we will certainly die]

14.q: וְ⁠כַ⁠מַּ֨יִם֙ הַ⁠נִּגָּרִ֣ים אַ֔רְצָ⁠ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר לֹ֣א יֵאָסֵ֑פוּ
14.note: The woman is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and we will die like water spilled on the ground that is not gathered]

14.q: וְ⁠כַ⁠מַּ֨יִם֙ הַ⁠נִּגָּרִ֣ים אַ֔רְצָ⁠ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר לֹ֣א יֵאָסֵ֑פוּ
14.note: The expressions **water spilled** and **is not gathered** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and we will die like water that someone has spilled on the ground that no one can gather up]

14.q: וְ⁠כַ⁠מַּ֨יִם֙ הַ⁠נִּגָּרִ֣ים אַ֔רְצָ⁠ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר לֹ֣א יֵאָסֵ֑פוּ
14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **water spilled on the ground** cannot be **gathered** up again, so a person who dies cannot be brought back to life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and after that we cannot be brought back to life]

The woman is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [but he makes merciful arrangements]

The expressions **the banished** and **will not be banished** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [so that people whom he has banished will not remain in banishment]

Here, the woman is speaking as if God had actually **banished** some people. She is referring to the way God works to restore people who have alienated themselves from him through sin and rebellion. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [to bring people back who have gone away from him]

15.note: The woman is using the term **word** to the case she presented by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to present my case]

The implication is that **the people** are specifically the members of the woman’s own clan. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the members of my clan]

15.q: וַ⁠תֹּ֤אמֶר שִׁפְחָֽתְ⁠ךָ֙ אֲדַבְּרָה־נָּ֣א אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ אוּלַ֛י יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶת־דְּבַ֥ר אֲמָתֽ⁠וֹ
15.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And I told myself that I should come and speak to you, since you might do what I requested]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:2. Alternate translation: [And your maidservant said to herself] or [And your maidservant thought]

The woman is using the term **word** to represent what she planned to say by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what his female servant asks] or [what I ask]

Here and in the next verse, the woman describes herself as a **female servant**, using a different term than the one she had been using, which the ULT translates as “maidservant.” This term refers to a higher-ranking member of the household whose master might feel some sense of obligation toward her. If your language and culture have different terms for female servants of different rank, use the term for a female servant of higher rank here and in the next verse.

16.q: כִּ֚י יִשְׁמַ֣ע הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ לְ⁠הַצִּ֥יל אֶת־אֲמָת֖⁠וֹ מִ⁠כַּ֣ף הָ⁠אִ֑ישׁ לְ⁠הַשְׁמִ֨יד אֹתִ֤⁠י וְ⁠אֶת־בְּנִ⁠י֙ יַ֔חַד מִֽ⁠נַּחֲלַ֖ת אֱלֹהִֽים
16.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate what the woman claims she said to herself so that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue to do that here.
See how you translated the similar expression in 12:18. Alternate translation: [will agree]

Here, **palm**, equivalent to “hand” in other contexts, represents the power and capability of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of the man]

The woman is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were something that Yahweh had inherited as a lasting possession. She is referring to the Israelites as the people who belong to Yahweh perpetually. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 10:1. Alternate translation: [from living among the people of Israel]

17.q: וַ⁠תֹּ֨אמֶר֙ שִׁפְחָ֣תְ⁠ךָ֔ יִֽהְיֶה־נָּ֛א דְּבַר־אֲדֹנִ֥⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ לִ⁠מְנוּחָ֑ה כִּ֣י ׀ כְּ⁠מַלְאַ֣ךְ הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֗ים כֵּ֣ן אֲדֹנִ֤⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֨עַ֙ הַ⁠טּ֣וֹב וְ⁠הָ⁠רָ֔ע
17.note: Some versions end the second-level quotation after **rest**. Alternate translation: [Then your maidservant said, ‘Now the word of my lord the king will be for rest.’ For like an angel of God, so {is} my lord the king, to understand good and evil]

17.q: יִֽהְיֶה־נָּ֛א דְּבַר־אֲדֹנִ֥⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ לִ⁠מְנוּחָ֑ה כִּ֣י ׀ כְּ⁠מַלְאַ֣ךְ הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֗ים כֵּ֣ן אֲדֹנִ֤⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֨עַ֙ הַ⁠טּ֣וֹב וְ⁠הָ⁠רָ֔ע
17.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since my lord the king is like an angel of God, to understand good and evil, now the word of my lord the king will be for rest]

The woman is using the term **word** to represent what the king would say by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what my lord the king tells me will be for rest]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rest**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will restore me to a restful situation]

Since the woman has already referred to David as **my lord the king** once in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun in this second instance. Alternate translation: [so is he]

The woman is asking God to bless King David. In your translation, use a form that people would recognize as a blessing in your language. You could express this as a prayer if that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I pray that Yahweh your God will continue to guide and support you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:12. Alternate translation: [And may Yahweh your God help you]

18.note: The expression **and said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly. Alternate translation: [And the king replied]

The woman is responding to David with a courteous expression that implies that she will answer truthfully. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Ask whatever you want, and I will tell you the truth]

19.note: The king is using **the hand of Joab** to represent Joab himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Is Joab with you in all this]
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:18. Alternate translation: [And the woman responded]

19.q: חֵֽי־נַפְשְׁ⁠ךָ֩ אֲדֹנִ֨⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֜לֶךְ אִם־אִ֣שׁ ׀ לְ⁠הֵמִ֣ין וּ⁠לְ⁠הַשְׂמִ֗יל מִ⁠כֹּ֤ל אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּר֙ אֲדֹנִ֣⁠י הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ
19.note: Following the custom of her culture, the woman is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred. She is then stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. In a context such as this, it may be natural to express just the first part of the condition as a negative statement. Alternate translation: [I swear by the life of your soul, my lord the king, that there is no turning to the right or turning to the left from all that my lord the king has spoken]

The woman is using **your soul** to represent David himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your life]

The woman is using **turning** in two basic directions, **the right** and **the left**, to represent all directions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [any turning away at all from anything]

Here, the woman is speaking of agreeing completely with the king’s words as if that were staying on a straight path and not **turning to the right or turning to the left**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [contradicting anything]
Here the word **For** provides not a reason but a further explanation. Alternate translation: [In fact,]

The woman is stating the pronoun **he** separately in both of these instances, even though the verbs translated as **he commanded** and **he put** already include this meaning. She is doing that to confirm Joab’s personal role in these actions. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for this same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that the woman is confirming Joab’s personal role. It may not be necessary to represent the separately stated pronouns explicitly. Alternate translation: [he was the one who commanded me, and he was the one who put]

19.q: שָׂ֚ם בְּ⁠פִ֣י שִׁפְחָֽתְ⁠ךָ֔ אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֖ים הָ⁠אֵֽלֶּה
19.note: Here, the woman is speaking as if words were actually objects that could be **put** in the **mouth** of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [told your maidservant everything she should say] or [told me everything I should say]

20.q: לְ⁠בַ⁠עֲב֤וּר סַבֵּב֙ אֶת־פְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠דָּבָ֔ר עָשָׂ֛ה עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֥ יוֹאָ֖ב אֶת־הַ⁠דָּבָ֣ר הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה
20.note: The woman is speaking as if the **matter** of Absalom’s banishment were a living thing that had a **face** that Joab could **turn**, in other words, as if Joab could get it to head in a different direction. This could mean: (1) that Joab wanted to change the situation so that Absalom could come home. Alternate translation: [In order to help Absalom come home from banishment, your servant Joab sent me to speak with you]; (2) that Joab told the woman to pretend to be a widow in order to make her appeal to David for Absalom appear to be an appeal for a son of her own. Alternate translation: [So that you would not realize I was talking about Absalom, your servant Joab told me to pretend I was talking about my own situation]

The woman is making an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. She could be saying: (1) that David knows what is happening in **the land**, that is, in the kingdom of Israel. Alternate translation: [since you clearly know what is happening in the land]; (2) that David knows everything that is happening on earth. Alternate translation: [as if you knew everything that was happening on earth]

21.note: Joab was clearly not present when the woman was speaking with David, since David had to ask her whether Joab had sent her to him. David must first have summoned Joab and then spoken to him as this verse describes. It may be appropriate in your language to reintroduce Joab as a participant in the story here. Alternate translation: [And the king summoned Joab and said to him]

22.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 14:4. Alternate translation: [And Joab bowed down all the way to the ground as a sign of deep respect]

The author does not mean that Joab gave David his blessing, since an inferior does not bless a superior. He means that Joab wished that Yahweh would bless David for agreeing that Absalom could return. In your translation, you may wish to represent what Joab may have said as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [and he said, “May Yahweh bless you, O king!”]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:19. Alternate translation: [you regard me with favor]

Here, **the word** represents what Joab said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what his servant has requested] or [what I, your servant, have requested]

23.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:14. Alternate translation: [And Joab took action]

24.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֤אמֶר הַ⁠מֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ יִסֹּ֣ב אֶל־בֵּית֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠פָנַ֖⁠י לֹ֣א יִרְאֶ֑ה
24.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

24.q: וּ⁠פָנַ֖⁠י לֹ֣א יִרְאֶ֑ה & וּ⁠פְנֵ֥י הַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ לֹ֥א רָאָֽה
24.note: Here, **face** represents the presence of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but he shall not come into my presence … but he did not come into the presence of the king]

25.q: וּ⁠כְ⁠אַבְשָׁל֗וֹם לֹא־הָיָ֧ה אִישׁ־יָפֶ֛ה בְּ⁠כָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְ⁠הַלֵּ֣ל מְאֹ֑ד
25.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. This verse describes Absalom’s outstanding physical appearance, which helps explain his popularity among the people and sets up his ability to gain followers later in the narrative. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

25.q: וּ⁠כְ⁠אַבְשָׁל֗וֹם לֹא־הָיָ֧ה אִישׁ־יָפֶ֛ה בְּ⁠כָל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְ⁠הַלֵּ֣ל מְאֹ֑ד
25.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Absalom being a handsome man with the information about people praising him. Alternate translation: [Now there was not another man in all of Israel whom people praised as greatly as they praised Absalom for being a handsome man]

25.q: מִ⁠כַּ֤ף רַגְל⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠עַ֣ד קָדְקֳד֔⁠וֹ לֹא־הָ֥יָה ב֖⁠וֹ מֽוּם
25.note: The author is referring to all of Absalom’s body by naming two extremes, **the sole of his foot** and **his pate**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He did not have a single blemish anywhere on his body]

25.q: מִ⁠כַּ֤ף רַגְל⁠וֹ֙ וְ⁠עַ֣ד קָדְקֳד֔⁠וֹ לֹא־הָ֥יָה ב֖⁠וֹ מֽוּם
25.note: The author is making an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [People felt that he was attractive in every part of his body]

26.q: וּֽ⁠בְ⁠גַלְּח⁠וֹ֮ אֶת־רֹאשׁ⁠וֹ֒ וְֽ֠⁠הָיָה מִ⁠קֵּ֨ץ יָמִ֤ים ׀ לַ⁠יָּמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יְגַלֵּ֔חַ כִּֽי־כָבֵ֥ד עָלָ֖י⁠ו וְ⁠גִלְּח֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠שָׁקַל֙ אֶת־שְׂעַ֣ר רֹאשׁ֔⁠וֹ מָאתַ֥יִם שְׁקָלִ֖ים בְּ⁠אֶ֥בֶן הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the initial statement about Absalom shaving his hair with the information about him weighing his hair. Alternate translation: [At the end of years to years he would shave, because it was heavy on him, so he would shave it. And when he shaved his head and weighed the hair of his head, it weighed 200 shekels by the stone of the king]

The author is using **at the end of years to years** as a common expression of his culture to mean “at the end of each year.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the end of each year]

The pronoun **it** refers in the first instance to Absalom’s hair and in the second instance to his head. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [because his hair heavy on him, so he would shave his head]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he found that it weighed 200 shekels by the stone of the king]
See the discussion of this phrase in the Introduction to this chapter for an explanation of what it might mean and for suggestions as to how you might represent it in your translation.

27.q: וַ⁠יִּֽוָּלְד֤וּ לְ⁠אַבְשָׁלוֹם֙ שְׁלוֹשָׁ֣ה בָנִ֔ים וּ⁠בַ֥ת אַחַ֖ת
27.note: The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And Absalom’s wife bore him three sons and one daughter]

28.note: The author is using **two years, days** as a common expression of his culture to mean “two full years.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [two full years]
See how you translated the similar expression in 14:24. Alternate translation: [but he did not come into the presence of the king]

29.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Joab, while the pronoun **him** refers to Absalom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but Joab was not willing to come to Absalom]

It might seem that the expression **Absalom sent again a second time** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [So Absalom sent for him again] or [So Absalom sent for him a second time]

30.note: Absalom is using the term **See** to focus his servants’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. See how you translated the similar expression in 7:2. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Absalom is using **to my hand** as a common expression of his culture to mean “next to mine.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is next to mine]

It might seem that the expression **burn it with fire** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it, here, in the next sentence, and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [Go and burn it] or [Go and set it on fire]

Here, the author is saying **the property** to represent the barley that was growing on the property. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the barley]

31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:14. Alternate translation: [And Joab took action]

Joab is using this expression to represent the barley on his **property**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the barley on my property]

32.q: הִנֵּ֣ה שָׁלַ֣חְתִּי אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ ׀ לֵ⁠אמֹ֡ר בֹּ֣א הֵ֠נָּה וְ⁠אֶשְׁלְחָה֩ אֹתְ⁠ךָ֨ אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֜לֶךְ לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר לָ֤⁠מָּה בָּ֨אתִי֙ מִ⁠גְּשׁ֔וּר ט֥וֹב לִ֖⁠י עֹ֣ד אֲנִי־שָׁ֑ם
32.note: There are three levels of quotation here. The author is quoting what Absalom said (level 1). Absalom is quoting what he sent his messengers to tell Joab on his behalf (level 2). And as he quotes their message, Absalom quotes what the messengers told Joab to say to King David on his behalf (level 3). Use the appropriate punctuation in your language to mark these levels of quotation. Alternatively, you could translate this so that there is not a second-level or third-level quotation (see the Quotes within Quotes note).

32.q: הִנֵּ֣ה שָׁלַ֣חְתִּי אֵלֶ֣י⁠ךָ ׀ לֵ⁠אמֹ֡ר בֹּ֣א הֵ֠נָּה וְ⁠אֶשְׁלְחָה֩ אֹתְ⁠ךָ֨ אֶל־הַ⁠מֶּ֜לֶךְ לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר לָ֤⁠מָּה בָּ֨אתִי֙ מִ⁠גְּשׁ֔וּר ט֥וֹב לִ֖⁠י עֹ֣ד אֲנִי־שָׁ֑ם
32.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Behold, I sent to you and told you to come here so that I could send you to the king and ask him on my behalf why I had come from Geshur, since it seemed as if it would be better for me if I were still there]

Absalom is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I should not have come from Geshur!]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce their main topic. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. See how you translated the same expression in 2:6.

Here, **the face of the king** represents “the presence of the king.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [arrange for me to come into the presence of the king]

Absalom is speaking as if iniquity were an object that was actually **in him**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but if I am guilty of a serious crime]

33.note: The pronoun **he** refers to King David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And King David called to Absalom]

33.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁתַּ֨חוּ ל֧⁠וֹ עַל־אַפָּ֛י⁠ו אַ֖רְצָ⁠ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י הַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ
33.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 14:4. Alternate translation: [and he bowed down with his face to the ground before the king]

Kissing Absalom was a symbolic action by which David expressed reconciliation and acceptance. After years of estrangement, this gesture demonstrated that David was officially forgiving his son and restoring him to his position in the royal family. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And the king kissed Absalom, signifying that he was restoring him to his position in the royal family]
